Article Title: Nestle dairy whitener found unsafe, substandard by FSSAI; Nestle says product safe
Article Text:
A Nestlé India spokesperson said phosphorus occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in milk-based products

NEW DELHI: A sample of Nestlé India’s Low Fat Dairy Whitener, collected from the premises of The LaLiT in Connaught Place, has been declared “unsafe and substandard” by a Food Analyst’s laboratory, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday.The sample was collected from M/s Bharat Hotels Ltd (The LaLiT), Connaught Place, FSSAI said. The regulator said the Food Analyst’s report found the product non-compliant under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said a copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator and a notice was issued regarding the non-compliant product. The operator was given an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst’s report within the prescribed period. FSSAI also directed that the identified product be immediately prohibited from sale.However, Nestlé India said the product is safe to consume and complies with all applicable regulatory requirements.A Nestlé India spokesperson said phosphorus occurs naturally in milk and is therefore present in milk-based products. The company said the FSSAI laboratory report reflects total phosphorus against the additive limit without accounting for the substantial natural phosphorus contribution from milk-based ingredients.Nestlé said the product is in full compliance with prescribed limits for added phosphorus under the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, including on an “as consumed” basis. The company said it has been engaging with the authorities through the due process established under law and has shared data on other same or similar milk-based products to demonstrate the presence of naturally occurring phosphorus.The LaLiT said the product was a packaged product procured from Nestlé India and that the sample was collected by FSSAI from the hotel approximately three months ago.Vivek Shukla, CEO, The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group, said that after receiving communication from FSSAI, the hotel immediately took up the matter with Nestlé India, which assured it that the company would respond directly to FSSAI.The hotel said it simultaneously discontinued use of the product and removed all packets from its operations.“The matter concerning the product’s compliance is between FSSAI and Nestlé India and not with The LaLiT,” Shukla said, adding that the hotel had acted promptly after receiving the communication and remained committed to food safety protocols and compliance with FSSAI regulations.FSSAI’s public communication does not specify the particular laboratory finding or parameter that led to the sample being classified as unsafe and substandard.
Article Summary: A sample of Nestlé India’s Low Fat Dairy Whitener has been declared ‘unsafe and substandard’ The sample was collected from M/s Bharat Hotels Ltd (The LaLiT), Connaught Place. Nestlé said the product is in full compliance with prescribed limits for added phosphorus.

Article Title: 'Had productive conversation': PM Modi speaks with US President Trump on trade, defence, energy
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday said that he had a "productive conversation" with US President Donald Trump and reviewed bilateral cooperation between New Delhi and Washington in various sectors.In a social media post on X, PM Modi said the leaders agreed to maintain close engagement to take their Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward."Had a productive conversation with President Trump. We reviewed our bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas. We agreed to maintain close engagement to take our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward," PM Modi said."We also exchanged views on regional and international issues, including ongoing efforts to advance global peace and security," he added.The two leaders agreed to remain in touch as both sides continue to deepen the strategic partnership.This comes days after Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia and Iran and giving his administration expanded powers to penalise countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas, including India.The legislation is particularly significant for India because it gives Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on imports from the five largest buyers of Russian oil or natural gas.India and China are among the major purchasers of Russian crude.Earlier in September, the ministry of external affairs warned the US of the legislation's potential impact on the US-India relationship."This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," the ministry had said.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi says he had a "productive conversation" with US President Donald Trump. The two leaders agreed to maintain close engagement to take their Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward. This comes days after Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia and Iran.

Article Title: ‘Journalists must be allowed to work freely’: Press Club 'shocked and dismayed' over Jantar Mantar police action
Article Text:
Delhi Police accused of misconduct with female journalist at Jantar Mantar.

Complaints trasferred to Crime Branch: Police

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Press Club of India has condemned the Delhi Police ’s alleged treatment of journalists and imposition of internet ban during protests at Jantar Mantar against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on Friday and Saturday, saying such behaviour “cannot be normalised in a democracy”.In a statement, the Press Club said it was “shocked and dismayed” by the police action against journalists covering the protests and raised concerns over media freedom in the national capital.“Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues,” the Press Club said, adding that the restrictions on journalists even in the heart of Delhi “do not bode well for the trajectory of media freedom in India”.The Press Club also urged the Delhi Police to immediately act on a complaint filed by a female journalist and ensure that mediapersons are able to perform their duties without facing “aggression and threats”.Eearlier in the day, Delhi Police said it had received complaints from three female journalists alleging sexual harassment during a protest in the New Delhi area on October 3. The complaints have been transferred to the Crime Branch at Kamla Market for further action, police said.Delhi Police X post reads, "On 03-10-26, during the protest in the New Delhi area, allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists in the context of the emergent law and order situation. New Delhi District has received their complaints and the same are transferred to Crime Branch, Kamla Market for further action."Jantar Mantar is witnessing protests demanding the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar over allegations concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Around 150 people demanding Kumar's removal were detained in and around Jantar Mantar on Saturday as security forces prevented protesters from gathering at the site.Those detained included senior advocates Prashant Bhushan and Kapil Sibal, Swaraj India founder Yogendra Yadav and AISA national president Neha Bora.
Article Summary: Delhi Police accused of misconduct with female journalist at Jantar Mantar. Delhi Police said it had received complaints from three female journalists alleging sexual harassment during a protest in the New Delhi area on October 3. The complaints have been transferred to the Crime Branch at Kamla Market for further action.

Article Title: 'Most comprehensive plan': Ukraine confirms India playing role in mediating energy truce in Black Sea
Article Text:
File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Picture credit: PTI)

India proposal among four initiatives

Kyiv backs safe Black Sea shipping

Also read:

Russia's position remains key to next steps

NEW DELHI: India's role in efforts to find a negotiated end to the Russia-Ukraine war has gained greater prominence, with Kyiv describing an Indian proposal as the most comprehensive among four initiatives currently under discussion and saying New Delhi has, for the first time, indicated its willingness to play an active mediating role.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha recently said Ukraine was prepared to consider both an energy and agricultural truce in the Black Sea, while also remaining open to an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact."We have four proposals. The most comprehensive is India's proposal. For the first time, India has signalled its willingness to play a role," Sybiha said during a press briefing, according to RBC Ukraine.According to Sybiha, four proposals are currently being considered in diplomatic efforts surrounding the war.India's proposal was described by the Ukrainian foreign minister as the most comprehensive.Türkiye and Egypt have separately proposed a grain and agricultural truce in the Black Sea, while the United States has put forward an energy truce proposal.The agricultural and maritime component is particularly important for Egypt, which relies on Ukrainian grain for roughly a third of its supply, according to RBC Ukraine.The US proposal on an energy truce was also discussed during a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump.Kyiv has conveyed its own approach to its partners and wants the energy and Black Sea components to be treated as an interconnected package.Sybiha said the energy component would require a complete halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, including port facilities.Ukraine has also expressed readiness for an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact. Sybiha said such a ceasefire could potentially emerge from a meeting between Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.The US is currently working actively on this diplomatic track, according to the Ukrainian foreign minister.The latest Ukrainian position builds on India's earlier engagement with Kyiv over restoring safe navigation in the Black Sea.During last month's UN General Assembly-related engagements, Zelenskyy said Egypt, India and Türkiye had put forward options for a maritime truce between Russia and Ukraine."We are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere," Zelenskyy said at the time.India has been engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv while advocating dialogue and diplomacy.External affairs minister S Jaishankar had said India was in continuous contact with both sides and was exploring ideas that could help mitigate and eventually end the conflict."If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said during his visit to Kyiv last month.During that visit, Jaishankar met Zelenskyy and Sybiha, with discussions covering peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, Black Sea navigation and global food security.Sybiha had also said Ukraine valued India's engagement in efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea."Restoring freedom of navigation is critical for global food security. Ukraine is ready to play a constructive role and we value India’s engagement," he said in a post on X.While Ukraine has indicated its readiness to consider multiple limited ceasefire arrangements, Russia's response remains central to whether the proposals can move forward.Sybiha's comments come amid differing assessments in Europe over Moscow's willingness to enter substantive peace negotiations.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently said Russia was not currently interested in genuine peace negotiations, while German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has expressed expectations that talks to end the war could begin in the near future.The Kremlin had previously said there were no prerequisites for moving towards a broader peace negotiating track while maintaining that Russia remained open to talks."For now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.Ukraine's latest position therefore places several limited ceasefire proposals, covering energy infrastructure, Black Sea shipping and agricultural supplies, alongside the possibility of a broader unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact.India's proposal is being considered alongside those initiatives, with Sybiha describing it as the most comprehensive and saying New Delhi has now signalled its readiness to play a role in the process.
Article Summary: India's proposal is described by the Ukrainian foreign minister as the most comprehensive. Türkiye and Egypt have separately proposed a grain and agricultural truce in the Black Sea. The United States has put forward an energy truce proposal. Russia's response remains central to whether the proposals can move forward.

Article Title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Article Text:
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi

Government targets legacy and fresh waste

New processing plants at three sites

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your top concern regarding pollution in Delhi? Landfill waste Air quality Water quality (Yamuna) Dust pollution 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years. She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure.

Article Title: SC steps in over relocation of 135-year-old Delhi library housing 8.5 lakh books
Article Text:

Court steps in over library's future

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognisance of the proposed relocation of Delhi's 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library, which holds more than 8.5 lakh books.The court's intervention comes amid reports that the library, currently located in Shastri Bhawan, has not been allotted space in the new Central Vista Plan. The building is proposed to be demolished as part of the Central Vista redevelopment.A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva is scheduled to hear the matter on Monday, October 5, reported LiveLaw.The suo motu case, titled "In Re: 135-Yr-Old Library 8.5 Lakh Books– And No Room In The New Central Vista Plan", was registered on October 3.The concerns centre on where the library and its vast collection of books would be housed if Shastri Bhawan is demolished. Reports said the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and the Central Public Works Department were still looking for suitable space for the library.The proposed relocation has also raised concerns about ensuring proper facilities for the preservation of its extensive collection.The Union ministry of housing and urban affairs, however, has rejected reports that the library has been left without space under the redevelopment plans."Contrary to a few reports, it is clarified that space for the Central Secretariat Library has been provided for in the Kartavya Path redevelopment plan. The necessary process for construction of the library is underway," the ministry wrote in a post on X.The ministry's statement indicates that a new location for the library has been included in the Kartavya Path redevelopment plan, although the Supreme Court is now set to examine the issue.
Article Summary: Supreme Court takes suo motu cognisance of proposed relocation of Delhi's 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library. Court's intervention comes amid reports that the library has not been allotted space in the new Central Vista Plan. A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva is scheduled to hear the matter on Monday.

Article Title: No room to roam: The cost of a crowded planet for wild animals
Article Text:
What shrinking habitats do to India's wildlife

A shrinking home, not a vanishing one

Not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life

What changes for an animal that loses space

Elephants outside the fence

The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants

Tigers on islands of forest

Where Kaziranga ends

The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve

Wetlands and the quieter losses

The cost to people

Where space is being rebuilt

What the evidence points to

Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out

Over the past fifty years, the average size of monitored wildlife populations around the world has fallen by 73 per cent, according to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024. The report names loss and degradation of habitat as the most commonly reported threat, driven mainly by how the world grows its food.This finding raises a plain question. When animals lose the land, water and forest they depend on, what happens to them?Habitat rarely disappears all at once. It is cut into pieces by farms, roads, canals, railway lines, power lines and growing towns. Each piece may still have trees and water, but it supports fewer animals than the original whole did.The 73 per cent figure also needs careful reading. It describes the average change across thousands of monitored populations. It does not mean that three-quarters of the world's animals are gone, or that three-quarters of species have disappeared. What it does show is a steady thinning, and the report describes such declines as an early warning of greater risk to species and ecosystems. The pressure it describes is gradual and widespread rather than the result of a single event, which is partly why it is easy to overlook. The report also notes that some populations have held steady or recovered where conservation has worked.“This is not just about wildlife, it’s about the essential ecosystems that sustain human life,” said Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF.The effects usually arrive in a recognisable order. Food and water become harder to find, so animals travel farther to reach them. Their routes cross fields, highways and railway tracks. Animals with large ranges, such as elephants and big cats, are affected first, because they need the most room.Smaller populations face a slower problem. When forest patches are cut off from one another, animals cannot move between them to find mates. Over time a small, isolated group becomes more vulnerable to disease and to sudden shocks such as drought or fire. Wherever forest meets farmland or settlement, animals and people also meet more often, and not always safely.India's elephants show how this plays out. The country holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants, according to the last census in 2017. Most of them do not live inside protected areas. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. That share matters for everything that follows. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.For these herds, a journey between feeding grounds can pass through paddy fields, village lanes, rail lines and overhead power cables. Official data tabled in Parliament in 2024 shows what that means. Over five years, the leading cause of unnatural elephant deaths was electrocution, ahead of train accidents, poaching and poisoning. Odisha, Assam, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu reported the largest numbers of electrocution deaths.The government has taken some steps in response. It has identified and ground-validated about 150 elephant corridors, the routes herds use to move between forests. The Railways and Environment ministries have also formed a standing committee to reduce deaths on tracks.Tigers tell a more hopeful story, with a warning attached. The 2022 estimate counted at least 3,682 tigers in India, a record, spread across 53 tiger reserves. These reserves are among the best protected forests in the country.But the same assessment shows the limits of protection. Roughly a third of the reserves need stronger protection, habitat restoration or more prey for the tigers to feed on. A few reserves in Mizoram, Nagaland and Jharkhand reported almost no tigers at all. Summaries of the report also describe many reserves as small islands of forest, joined to one another by a limited number of corridors. A reserve with a healthy tiger population can send young animals out in search of territory of their own, and many of them end up in unprotected land among farms and villages.The record count and the weak reserves belong in the same account. Protection works where it is applied well, and the gaps appear where it is not.Kaziranga's protection does not stop at the park boundary, and a new proposal from the Assam government has put that line under debate. The state wants to replace the default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific zone of one to three kilometres. An ESZ is a regulatory buffer, declared by the environment ministry on a state's proposal. It is not an outright ban: depending on the notification, activities in it may be prohibited, regulated or permitted, and mining is among those most strictly restricted.Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma says the 10-km limit applies only because Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified. He argues it brings populated areas such as Kaliabor, Doboka and Jakhalabandha under restrictions, and holds up civic projects like a proposed stadium in Bokakhat. The state says the park's boundary and its UNESCO World Heritage status will not change, and that the 10-km zone stays in force until a new one is notified. Some residents agree. Hundreds rallied in support of the proposal on August 18, saying the current limits get in the way of building homes and basic infrastructure.The opposition and conservationists are not convinced. Congress state president Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and alleged that the change could give legal cover to mining. The state government rejects the charge. Conservationists such as Jadav Payeng and Kavita Ashok point to the annual floods, when rhinos, deer and elephants move to higher ground outside the park. A smaller zone, they warn, could cut off those routes.A 2025 conservation assessment notes that a smaller zone is not necessarily a weaker one if it is designed to protect the most sensitive areas. Whether it does will depend on the final notification, which will decide whether wildlife corridors, flood escape routes and wetlands fall inside the line.Space does not only mean forest. Globally, freshwater species have seen the steepest declines in the WWF report, and wetlands are often among the first places to be drained or built over.The report points to Chennai, where rapid urban growth has led to a large loss of wetland area. Wetlands shelter birds, fish and amphibians, and they also soak up floodwater for the city around them. When they go, wildlife loses a home and people lose a buffer.When space runs out, people pay too. Government data tabled in Parliament showed that elephants killed 2,853 people in India over five years, with the highest toll in 2023. Many of these deaths happened in places where farms, villages and elephant routes overlap. The elephant deaths and the human deaths come from the same stretches of land, where both now depend on the same ground.The Environment Ministry has issued guidelines on managing human-elephant conflict, and it says compensation is provided for losses. These measures respond to the damage after it happens. They do not by themselves restore the space that animals have lost.Some efforts aim at the cause. West Bengal has begun a community programme called Gajamitra, or Friends of Elephants, in which local people take part in reducing conflict. Conservation scientists have also suggested low-cost methods for farmers, such as planting chillies, ginger or citrus around fields, which elephants tend to avoid, or placing beehives along field edges.The WWF report also records progress in India, where it says some wildlife populations have stabilised or recovered. It credits government initiatives, careful habitat management, scientific monitoring and community involvement. At the global level, the report calls for more effective conservation along with changes in food, energy and finance systems.The picture from India and from the world is consistent. Animals do not simply move on when their habitat shrinks. Their numbers thin out, they wander into danger, they come into conflict with people, or they disappear from places they once held. Where land is protected, connected and shared with the people who live beside it, some populations hold their ground or recover.India's own examples point in both directions: electrocutions and train deaths on one side, a record tiger count and recovering populations on the other. The difference lies largely in whether land is protected and linked together, and whether the people who live beside wildlife are part of the plan.The question on World Wildlife Day is how much room is left for wildlife, and who decides what happens to it.
Article Summary: India holds about 60 per cent of the world's Asian elephants. Government and press figures put the share outside reserves at about 80 per cent. A herd that lives mostly outside reserves has no boundary between it and the land that people farm, travel across and build on.

Article Title: Insurance companies want policyholders to pay 10% of health claims
Article Text:
The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals.

Outpatient claims would remain outside scheme

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: Non-life insurers are considering a 10% co-payment by policyholders on retail health policies from Jan 1, 2027, with the patient's contribution capped at Rs 5 lakh per claim. In return, customers would pay lower annual premiums.The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals. The arrangement would require even those with comprehensive health insurance to keep funds for medical emergencies, as they would have to pay 10% of admissible inpatient hospitalisation costs, including those arising from accidents, whether claims are settled through cashless procedure or reimbursement.The proposal covers retail indemnity products, retail-under-group policies, indemnity components of combi products, internal migrations and portability business. Outpatient claims would remain outside the scheme.Co-payment cannot be waived, reduced or modified through riders or endorsements, and the customer’s 10% contribution cannot be recovered from another health insurance policy.“The choice between a cheaper policy with a deductible and a full-compensation policy should rest with the insured.People buy insurance to be indemnified for their costs. It would be unfair to customers willing to pay a higher premium for a higher sum insured to still bear part of the cost, and this could discourage them from buying high-value policies,” said Shreeraj Deshpande, a health insurance expert who earlier headed operations at a general insurer. While the industry is seeking to address what it sees as cost distortions in healthcare, some fear a mandatory requirement could be anti-competitive. “If the industry collectively decides that no one will offer a full-compensation policy, it might catch the attention of the Competition Commission,” said an industry executive.The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover. Higher-category rooms can also increase total bills because doctors’ fees and procedure charges are often linked to room tariffs.With insurance covering the full bill, patients may have less incentive to question charges or choose lower-cost hospitals.“This behaviour (overbilling and provider-induced demand) stems from the perception that insurance-backed patients are less price-sensitive, leading to inflated healthcare costs,” a council note said.The proposal also calls for common hospital empanelment, outcome-based contracts and a payor-provider grievance forum. GI Council plans standard empanelment across more than 4,300 hospitals to set benchmark tariffs and curb arbitrary billing, while linking contracts to clinical and procedure-wise outcomes.
Article Summary: Non-life insurers are considering a 10% co-payment by policyholders on retail health policies from Jan 1, 2027. The patient's contribution would be capped at Rs 5 lakh per claim. In return, customers would pay lower annual premiums.

Article Title: PK Mishra: India must stay open, but not become vulnerable
Article Text:
PK Mishra said the world in the near future will belong to those who can be steady without being closed and ambitious without being naive, and India aims to be such a country.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India needs to remain open to the world without becoming “excessively vulnerable” to the globe amid export restrictions, sanctions and tariffs being weaponised, principal secretary to PM PK Mishra said on Saturday.At the Kautilya Economic Conclave, Mishra said the changing nature of trade policy was adding to uncertainty for economies. “The question before policymakers is not whether globalisation has ended... The question is how we preserve the gains from openness while making economies less vulnerable to concentrated and unpredictable shocks.” The economic logic of globalisation was built around specialisation and production where costs are lowest, and goods move efficiently across borders.He said the logic remains “relevant” and even powerful.He said the world in the near future will belong to those who can be steady without being closed and ambitious without being naive, and India aims to be such a country.Speaking at the event, VP CP Radhakrishnan said it is essential that the fruits of development reach everyone, failing which youth may lose faith in democracy.
Article Summary: PK Mishra said the changing nature of trade policy was adding to uncertainty for economies. The economic logic of globalisation was built around specialisation and production where costs are lowest, and goods move efficiently across borders. He said the world in the near future will belong to those who can be steady without being closed and ambitious without being naive.

Article Text:
According to CBI, its investigation revealed that in 2012, LIC subscribed to Non-Convertible Debentures worth Rs 1,500 crore issued by Reliance Communications Ltd. based on serious misrepresentations.

NEW DELHI: CBI has filed a chargesheet against Reliance Communications Ltd and three key executives in a Rs 3,750 crore fraud case alleged by Life Insurance Corporation (LIC). The document names Amitabh Jhunjhunwala, Group MD of Reliance ADA Group, Vishwas Joshi, senior VP of Reliance Capital Limited, and P Venugopal, the then chief investment officer of LIC. CBI filed its report before the special judge for CBI cases in Mumbai.The accused have been charged with offences of criminal conspiracy, cheating, and criminal breach of trust under IPC sections, alongside charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act.According to CBI, its investigation revealed that in 2012, LIC subscribed to Non-Convertible Debentures worth Rs 1,500 crore issued by Reliance Communications Ltd. based on serious misrepresentations."The funds received from the subscription were subsequently diverted to other Reliance ADA Group companies, resulting in wrongful gain to the accused while causing a total alleged loss of ₹3,750 crore to LIC," CBI has said in the chargesheet.The probe agency had registered this case on April 1, 2026, following a complaint lodged by LIC. This submission represents the eighth chargesheet filed by the agency in a broader crackdown on Reliance ADA Group entities.CBI has registered nine FIRs against Reliance Communications Limited, Reliance Home Finance Limited and other group entities. These FIRs stem from complaints by various public sector banks, LIC and Employees' Provident Fund Organisation. Seven have been arrested in these cases.

NEW DELHI: RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday said the Indian financial system remained resilient and the economy had navigated the West Asia crisis well, but policymakers needed to stay vigilant."We cannot afford to become complacent; the economic and financial costs of allowing vulnerabilities to build up are simply too high... Today's resilience may not necessarily imply tomorrow's immunity. We are committed to remaining vigilant of emerging vulnerabilities and continuing to keep our financial system strong and resilient," he said at the Kautilya Economic Conclave, organised by the Institute of Economic Growth and the finance ministry.He cautioned against the possible adverse impact of the war in Iran, which has hit supply chains. "The financial system has absorbed the supply shock due to the West Asia conflict well. However, the global economic environment remains challenging. The conflict has exacerbated inflationary pressures and enhanced financial system vulnerabilities," the RBI governor said, adding India was navigating from a position of strength.Malhotra cautioned against stressed valuations, especially those related to AI, elevated debt levels globally, elevated leverage that could spill over to banks and markets in case of tightening of financial conditions, private credit, and cyber risks that have been compounded by AI."Strong macroeconomic fundamentals and a resilient financial system provide confidence in our ability to withstand this lingering shock. At the same time, we are taking further measures to enhance our resilience to such shocks," he said, listing diversification of import sources, greater self-sufficiency in energy and other critical resources, enhancing manufacturing competitiveness, expanding market access through free trade agreements, and promoting trade settlement in local currencies, among others.The RBI governor also said Indian bond yields had risen only partially in response to higher global energy prices and global yields, reflecting the prudence in fiscal management, credible monetary policy and declining structural pressure on inflation.He said the Indian private credit market remained small, equity markets had corrected in recent months, and cyber risk governance had been strengthened. "Overall, the financial system is assessed to be very resilient, supported by healthy balance sheets of banks and NBFIs," Malhotra said.
Article Summary: RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said the Indian financial system remained resilient and the economy had navigated the West Asia crisis well. He cautioned against stressed valuations, especially those related to AI, elevated debt levels globally, elevated leverage that could spill over to banks.

Article Title: Resource security key as global economy faces uncertainty: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman
Article Text:
The remarks assume significance amid global economic uncertainties triggered by US tariffs and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, which have disrupted global supply chains and resulted in higher prices of key commodities.

NEW DELHI: Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Saturday said that amid uncertainty, “now a standing condition” of the global economy, national security requires structural autonomy in strategic inputs, as strategic resource security sits at the centre of macroeconomic policy.Besides, she argued for private investment to lead the cycle, including in research and innovation and skilling to prepare people for a changing world of work, while asserting that global financial architecture should reflect where growth was coming from.“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it’s not a one-time exercise. The coming years call for preparation, and India approaches them from strength,” she said at Kautilya Economic Conclave.The remarks assume significance amid global economic uncertainties triggered by US tariffs and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, which have disrupted global supply chains and resulted in higher prices of key commodities.“A price shock can be cushioned with monetary and fiscal tools. But a quantity shock tests buffer stocks and the reach of delivery systems and therefore the capacity of the state itself,” she added.Sitharaman said supply chains optimised for cost alone carry hidden fragility. To replace fragile single-source dependencies with domestic operational depth, the government has launched programmes focused on critical minerals and rare earths, semiconductors and small modular nuclear reactors.She said for India, resilience means building upon the structural foundations laid over the past decade such as entrepreneurial growth, focusing on efficient last-mile delivery, infrastructure creation and managing prices, essential supplies and external pressures. “The test of the coming years will again be partly invisible: the shocks India absorbs without disruption to households and enterprises.”The evidence of resilience lies in the counterfactual, in the outcomes that did not materialise, such as an inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at the fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced. “These counterfactuals deserve as much attention from economists as the headline growth rate,” she added.Talking about open, predictable and rule-based global economic relationships, Sitharaman said nations should engage with one another through dialogue and negotiated agreements, rather than allowing geopolitical differences to become barriers to trade and investment.

The coming years call for preparation, and India approaches them from strength,” she said.

Article Title: Hormuz blocked, but Gulf crude shipments at pre-war level
Article Text:
Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.

Crude via other routes made up the difference

325 million barrels released from oil reserves: IEA

Disruptions to energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz notwithstanding, crude shipments from the West Asian Gulf region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels as countries cut dependence on oil tankers to navigate through the choked strait. According to maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the prewar average. During the peak of the West Asia war in March, the average was 10.5 mbd.While 83% of the region’s crude crossed Hormuz before the war, 40% was exported in Sept through pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE without crossing the key chokepoint.Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.Belostrino said more than 70% of the crude that crossed the Strait of Hormuz in Aug changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman.Confirmed crude crossings were still more than a quarter below the pre-war level, but volumes moving through alternative routes had more than doubled and made up almost exactly the difference. Saudi pushed more crude through the east-west pipeline to Yanbu, with loadings rising from 0.8 mbd before the war to 4.3 mbd in June. UAE sent crude through the Abu Dhabi crude oil pipeline to Fujairah, where loadings rose from 1.1 mbd to 2.7 mbd.The International Energy Agency said member countries had released 325 million barrels of oil and oil products from strategic reserves, out of 400 million barrels pledged in March.
Article Summary: Crude shipments from the West Asian Gulf region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels. According to maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the prewar average.

Article Title: Indians live longer than Pakistanis, lag Bangladeshis, says WHO
Article Text:
The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover.

In 2 years from 2021, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan: WHO

NEW DELHI: Indians can expect to live longer than their counterparts in Pakistan, but have shorter lives than people in Bangladesh, the US and Canada, according to the latest World Health Organization estimates.India's life expectancy at birth was 71 years in 2023, compared with 68.2 years in Pakistan, 72.7 years in Bangladesh, 78.5 years in the US and 81.4 years in Canada. But living longer does not necessarily mean living more years in good health. India's healthy life expectancy was 60.6 years in 2023, compared with 60.5 in 2019. It had fallen to 58.4 years in 2021 before recovering to 60.2 years in 2022. The figures are part of WHO's Global Health Estimates, released Friday, covering life expectancy, healthy life expectancy, causes of death and disease burden from 2000 to 2023. WHO said global life expectancy recovered close to pre-pandemic levels, while healthy life expectancy has recovered more slowly.For India, the difference is particularly visible over the pandemic years. Life expectancy fell from 70.5 years in 2019 to 68.1 years in 2021 before rising to 70.5 years in 2022 and 71 years in 2023. In just two years, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan.Healthy life expectancy, however, recovered by only 2.2 years, from 58.4 years in 2021 to 60.6 years in 2023, leaving it just 0.1 year above the 2019 level.The gap is also visible among older Indians. At age 60, a person could expect another 18.8 years of life in 2023, compared with 18.4 years in 2019. But 13.7 of those years were expected to be lived in full health, up from 13.4 years in 2019.India’s disease profile has changed sharply. Communicable diseases, such as tuberculosis and diarrhoeal infections, can spread from person to person, while non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as heart disease, stroke and diabetes, are generally long-term conditions.In 2000, communicable diseases accounted for nearly 62% of the combined death rate from the country’s 10 leading causes, while NCDs accounted for 34%. By 2023, the pattern had reversed, with NCDs accounting for nearly 75% and communicable diseases 16% of the combined death rate from the top 10 causes. The rest was from injuries.The shift is evident in the leading causes. In 2000, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal diseases topped the list, with 92.4 and 87.8 deaths per 100,000 population. By 2023, ischaemic heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke and diabetes were among the leading causes, with rates of 138.5, 83.19, 74.8 and 49.01, respectively. Yet infectious diseases remain a significant burden, with diarrhoeal diseases, tuberculosis and lower respiratory infections still among India’s top 10 causes of death in 2023.Globally, the shift towards chronic diseases is also pronounced. NCDs accounted for 74% of deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000, while eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs. Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, almost back to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019, while healthy life expectancy stood at 62.8 years, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.
Article Summary: India's life expectancy at birth was 71 years in 2023, compared with 68.2 years in Pakistan, 72.7 years in Bangladesh, 78.5 years in the US and 81.4 years in Canada. In 2 years from 2021, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan: WHO. Living longer does not necessarily mean living more years in good health.

NEW DELHI: ‘Road injuries’ was the eighth leading cause of deaths among males in India in 2023, and in the case of females, ‘falls’ was the eighth biggest cause of deaths, as per the latest WHO Global Health Estimates (GHE). Overall, road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th.India, which has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started, registered 1.74 lakh such fatalities in 2023, and this was a little over 14% of the 12.2 lakh people who lost their lives in road crashes across the world. This has only increased in the past two years to reach 1.83 lakh in 2025. The figures underline the continuing scale of the road safety challenge in the country, where road crashes claim 500 lives daily.Falls in India claimed 25,150 lives, as per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, which was around 3% of the total 8.42 lakh lives lost in such incidents. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable. The data also highlights the significant burden of injuries that can result in loss of life and have wider social and economic consequences for families.As per the WHO report, globally, road traffic injuries were the 8th biggest cause of death in low-income countries and the 10th biggest in middle-income countries. Globally, it was ranked 11th, indicating that the high number of such deaths not only has a huge burden on low- and middle-income countries but also a major concern for the global community, despite many developed nations having been successful in bringing down fatalities due to road crashes.The differences in rankings across income groups also reflect the varying burden of road injuries across countries and regions.Road safety experts have maintained that low- and middle-income countries need to find solutions to this “avoidable disaster” taking into account the local conditions, including heterogeneous road users and poorly sensitised authorities about the concept of safety of all users. They said addressing the problem would require greater attention to the safety needs of different categories of road users and a stronger focus on preventing crashes and reducing their consequences.
Article Summary: India has recorded the maximum road deaths since such global data compilation started. Road traffic injuries ranked the 10th leading cause of death for both males and females in India, while fatalities due to falls ranked 9th. Most of the deaths due to road crashes and falls are preventable.

Article Title: Helicopters, influencers and nail art: The money trail of 2026 assembly elections
Article Text:
The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns.

The campaign war chests

Different states, different stakes

A statewise representation of poll expenditure by the BJP and Congress.

Ads, aircraft and the spending gap

The funding gap between BJP and Congress, and where the money was spent.

From nail art to AI calls

When spending and seats diverged

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From paying social-media influencers to allocating money for 'nail art', the BJP 's expenditure statements reveal the range of campaign activities funded during its bid to win the West Bengal assembly election. A closer look at political parties' filings with the Election Commission of India (ECI) makes for interesting reading, revealing how spending priorities varied according to the political stakes in different states. However, the TVK example is only a humbling reminder that in democracy, greater outreach may lead to greater eyeballs, but it is no guarantee for success.The BJP declared Rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Congress declared Rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount.A TOI analysis of the expenditure filings shows that Rs 178.78 crore of the Rs 280.84-crore difference, nearly two-thirds, came from advertisements and travel by star campaigners, the top leaders a party sends around a state to address rallies. Money given directly to candidates accounted for only Rs 16.27 crore of the gap. At least on paper, the BJP's extensive advertising campaigns and deployment of senior leaders, many of them massive crowd pullers, distinguished its expenditure pattern from that of Congress.The BJP won 207 seats in West Bengal in the results declared on May 4 and later won the Falta repoll to take its tally to 208. It formed its first government in the state, ending the Trinamool Congress's 15-year rule. TMC chief Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat, Bhabanipur, to the BJP's Suvendu Adhikari. The BJP-led NDA won Assam for a third consecutive term, while the NDA led by the All India NR Congress retained Puducherry.In Keralam, the Congress-led UDF returned to power after 10 years. Congress won 63 of the 140 seats, the CPI(M)-led LDF 35 and the BJP three. In Tamil Nadu, film star Vijay's TVK, contesting its first assembly election on the whistle symbol, won 108 of the 234 seats, ahead of the DMK with 59 and the AIADMK with 47. Subsequently, Vijay became chief minister.The BJP, Congress and CPI(M) filed accounts covering all five elections, with the CPI(M) declaring only Rs 39.04 crore as expenditure. The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore spending for Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore expenses in a statement covering Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Keralam.TVK reported Rs 19.81 crore for Tamil Nadu, according to TOI report. TMC's full 2026 expenditure statement is not available on the ECI website.Political parties have no overall election expenditure ceiling, but individual candidates face spending limits. The accounts can also include expenditure authorised but not yet paid. The BJP's Bengal return, for instance, recorded Rs 89.32 crore in outstanding general-campaign expenditure at the end of the election period.More than half the BJP's money, Rs 286.99 crore or 54.2 per cent, went to Bengal, followed by Rs 96.27 crore in Assam. Together, the two states accounted for Rs 383.26 crore, or 72.4 per cent of the party's total. The BJP also declared Rs 82.67 crore in Keralam, Rs 51.56 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.90 crore in Puducherry.The spending pattern broadly reflected the different political stakes.The figure broadly aligns with what was at stake too. BJP was desperate to get power in Bengal after catapulting to second position in 2021 and sensing anti-incumbency was heavily weighing down on Mamata Banerjee. In Assam, it was looking to consolidate a strong position. The party had much less at stake in Tamil Nadu where it is still an emerging force. In Keralam, a much smaller state than Tamil Nadu, more amount was pumped in sensing an opportunity to break the binary nature of the state politics.For Congress, the situation was totally different. Its biggest chance for coming to power was in Keralam and it’s no surprise that the party spent the most in Keralam, Rs 105.34 crore or 42.4 per cent of its total, followed by Assam at Rs 67.62 crore, or 27.2 per cent. It declared Rs 42.08 crore in Bengal, Rs 22.25 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.25 crore in Puducherry.Bengal accounts for most of the gap between the two parties, perhaps unsurprisingly, although both parties were contesting almost the same number of seats in the state. The BJP declared Rs 244.91 crore more than Congress there, about 87 per cent of the total difference. Keralam was the only state where Congress declared more, by Rs 22.67 crore.Party filings divide spending into different categories, and three of them help explain the BJP–Congress difference to an extent.The BJP declared Rs 187.54 crore on general-party media advertisements, which promote the party as a whole rather than individual candidates. Congress declared Rs 92.52 crore, a difference of Rs 95.02 crore.Star-campaigner travel covers trips by a party's senior leaders, and the BJP's schedules list aircraft and helicopter travel for several of them. The BJP declared Rs 106.25 crore under this head against Congress's Rs 22.49 crore, about 4.7 times as much and Rs 83.76 crore more.Direct grants, the money a party transfers to candidates, were much closer. The BJP declared Rs 111.79 crore and Congress Rs 95.52 crore, a difference of Rs 16.27 crore, with the BJP's grants about 17 per cent higher. Congress spent slightly more on grants than on general-party media advertisements.In Bengal, the BJP recorded grants of Rs 20 lakh each to its 294 candidates, totalling Rs 58.80 crore. In the same state, it declared Rs 88.48 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 52.18 crore on star-campaigner travel.Grants, however, are only part of the support candidates receive, since parties also pay centrally for publicity, rallies and other campaign activities.The difference extended beyond advertisements and star campaigners' travel. The BJP declared ₹52.34 crore on publicity materials, including posters, banners and flags, against Congress's ₹11.48 crore. Under other general-party expenses, the BJP recorded ₹48.83 crore against Congress's ₹6.78 crore, another ₹42.05-crore gap. Congress, however, declared more expenditure on general-party meetings and rallies, ₹7.99 crore against the BJP's ₹4.06 crore.The filings name the people and firms that were paid, though they do not always specify what services were delivered.In Bengal, the BJP's accounts include payments recorded against social-media influencers and content creators. TOI earlier reported that influencer Sayak Chakraborty acknowledged receiving Rs 2.5 lakh for two videos, The Bengal accounts also contain entries for nail art. Four entries of Rs 1 lakh each, marked "Nail Art", appear under public meetings and rallies. Another Rs 9.65 lakh is recorded against Visionary Edge for a "Nail Art Prog" under media advertisements.Sayak was not the only influencer or content creator named in the accounts. Others have also acknowledged receiving payments. Yet the separate virtual-campaign schedules recorded no expenditure.Across the five elections, the BJP's accounts list Rs 41.83 crore against Google India and Rs 15.65 crore against Facebook India Online Services, a total of Rs 57.48 crore, of which Rs 31.39 crore was attributed to Bengal. This amount is already included in the BJP's advertising expenditure. Advertising purchased through agencies for social media may also appear under other names.The filings also point to the use of artificial intelligence in election outreach. Congress's headquarters recorded Rs 3.72 crore against Neomarq Flare Solution LLP in Assam for a service described as "AI 2 Way Voice Calling".In Tamil Nadu, the DMK's Rs 197.85 crore included Rs 70.63 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 45.75 crore in grants to candidates. Five entries marked "Social media" added up to Rs 16.87 crore, naming Vipras Ads, Ravi Publicity Services, Glovy Trading and Populus Empowerment Network.Populus appeared four times in the accounts, for manpower and consultancy, campaign production, digital advertising (Rs 6.37 crore) and social media. Together, these entries totalled Rs 74.94 crore, about 37.9 per cent of the DMK's expenditure.The AIADMK recorded Rs 103.99 crore of its Rs 112.40 crore, or 92.5 per cent, in a single entry for Pramanya Strategy Consulting, described as "Social Media Promotion, TV, Website". Because the filing does not break down this amount, it cannot be compared directly with the DMK's specifically labelled social-media entries.The CPI(M)'s Keralam unit accounted for Rs 28.60 crore of the party's Rs 39.04 crore, and its Bengal unit Rs 8.23 crore. In Keralam, the party recorded Rs 19.53 crore on general-party media advertisements, of which Rs 18.77 crore, about 96 per cent, appeared in four entries naming Maitri Advertising for print, television and electronic media.These entries identify the companies named in the expenditure schedules, not necessarily the ultimate media outlets or platforms.The BJP won Bengal, the state where it declared its largest expenditure, while the Congress-led UDF won Keralam, where Congress spent the most.Tamil Nadu, however, presented a striking contrast.TVK reported expenditure of Rs 19.81 crore, including about Rs 6.3 crore on media advertisements, Rs 3.5 crore on Vijay's air travel and Rs 2.1 crore on public meetings and roadshows, according to TOI's September 26 report.The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore in a statement covering three jurisdictions. Although the reporting coverage differed, TVK's declared expenditure was substantially smaller than that of either established Dravidian party.Yet TVK won 108 assembly seats, compared with the DMK's 59 and the AIADMK's 47.Vijay entered politics with a considerable advantage in public recognition, having spent decades as one of Tamil cinema's biggest stars. His existing fan base and celebrity appeal may have given TVK organic visibility, yet the difference in spendings can’t be ignored.The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns, from helicopters and digital advertisements to influencers, consultants and AI-powered calls. They also expose the limits of pumping funds to win elections. Hence Tamil Nadu perhaps had the most important lesson for mainstream political parties.
Article Summary: BJP declared Rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Congress declared Rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount. BJP's extensive advertising campaigns and deployment of senior leaders distinguished its expenditure pattern from that of Congress.

Article Title: 'No deadline for Sheikh Hasina's return', says Indian high commissioner in Bangladesh

“At that point in time, Hasina was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that”, Trivedi said (Photo credit: AP).

Strained ties
